Process.definition: A program in execution; an instance of a running program that includes the program code, data, stack, heap, and process control block.

Thread.definition: A lightweight process that shares the address space and resources of its parent process but maintains its own program counter, registers, and stack.

CPU Scheduling.definition: The activity of the operating system that decides which process or thread to run next on the CPU.

Process Synchronization.definition: The coordination of concurrent processes to ensure that they access shared resources in a mutually exclusive and orderly fashion.

Context Switch.definition: The mechanism of storing and restoring the state of a process or thread so that it can be resumed from the same point later.

Scheduler.definition: The component of the operating system that selects which process or thread to execute next.

Preemptive Scheduling.definition: A scheduling policy that allows the operating system to interrupt a running process and allocate the CPU to another process.

Non-preemptive Scheduling.definition: A scheduling policy in which a process keeps the CPU until it terminates or voluntarily yields it.

Race Condition.definition: A situation in which the outcome of a computation depends on the relative timing of concurrent events, leading to unpredictable results.

Critical Section.definition: A segment of code that accesses shared resources and must be executed by only one process at a time.

Mutex.definition: A synchronization primitive that provides mutual exclusion; only one thread can hold it at a time.

Semaphore.definition: A synchronization primitive that uses a counter to control access to a set of resources; supports wait and signal operations.

Monitor.definition: A high-level synchronization construct that encapsulates shared data and the operations that access it, ensuring mutual exclusion.

Memory Management.definition: The set of techniques and mechanisms used by an operating system to allocate, deallocate, and organize main memory among competing processes and to abstract the underlying physical memory into a usable resource.

Virtual Memory.definition: An abstraction that extends the address space of processes beyond the size of physical RAM by using secondary storage, allowing processes to use memory addresses that are mapped to physical memory or disk.

Page.definition: A fixed-size block of contiguous memory used as the basic unit of data movement between physical memory and secondary storage.

Page Table.definition: A data structure maintained by the operating system that maps virtual pages of a process to their corresponding physical frames in memory.

Frame.definition: A fixed-size block of physical memory that holds a single page.

Swap Space.definition: An area on secondary storage (disk) used by the operating system to store pages that are not currently in physical memory.

File.definition: A named collection of related data stored on secondary storage, identified by a pathname, and accessed via I/O operations.

Directory.definition: A special file that contains a set of file names and their associated metadata, used to organize files hierarchically.

Block.definition: A fixed-size unit of data storage, typically 512 bytes or 4096 bytes, that forms the basic building block of a file system.

Inode.definition: A data structure in a file system that stores metadata about a file, such as its size, permissions, and pointers to its data blocks.

Device Driver.definition: A software component that controls a hardware device, providing a standardized interface to the operating system and applications.

Interrupt.definition: A signal to the processor that indicates the occurrence of an event requiring immediate attention, causing the CPU to temporarily halt its current execution and transfer control to a handler.

Case Study.definition: A detailed examination of a specific instance or scenario that illustrates broader operating system concepts.

Laboratory.definition: A structured environment or set of activities that allows students to apply theoretical concepts to practical tasks, often using simulated or real hardware.

Hands‑on.definition: Direct, interactive engagement with computing resources to observe outcomes and reinforce learning.

Simulation.definition: The abstraction of a real‑world process or system using a computational model to study behavior without physical implementation.

Exercise.definition: A task or problem designed to reinforce understanding of a specific concept or technique, often requiring execution or analysis.

Practical Lab Work.definition: A curriculum component that combines hands‑on activities with guided instructions to explore operating system functionalities.
